items: RoboJEPA reports scaling trends for fixed-encoder robotic latent world models — importance 6/10 · The RoboJEPA authors report that scaling a latent-dynamics predictor trained over a fixed pretrained visual encoder improves prediction and downstream planning across a collection of robot datasets. The paper evaluates 22M–8B parameter predictors using 23 public manipulation datasets spanning 12 embodiments and 26 action spaces, and reports more than 50,000 evaluation episodes across two platforms. Its real-robot results are narrower: a Franka setup with ten episodes per task, where larger models do not improve every task uniformly. These are paper-reported results without independent replication; the scaling claim does not include jointly scaling the visual encoder. — FCMO-7464B9E4FD57

Execution-improved robot software transfers better than initial code on a small simulated task suite — importance 5/10 · A Sakana AI preprint treats complete closed-loop robot programs as reusable execution experience: coding agents revise source-task policies using simulator feedback, then retain the selected code as reference material for new tasks. In RoboCasa, the authors report mean test success rising from 28.3% for initial code to 64.2% after iterative optimization across four source tasks. Across nine target tasks and three policy-generation runs, optimized references reach a 57.0% nine-task mean, versus 41.5% with initial references and 45.2% without references. The result is a paper-reported simulation finding; physical-robot transfer is untested and optimized references do worse on two of nine target tasks. — FCMO-15B24053E1A4

items: EU Commission announces a Scientific Panel meeting on frontier AI risks after loss-of-control investigations — importance 5/10 · In a 9 October press release, the Commission says its 60-member AI Act Scientific Panel had investigated recent loss-of-control incidents and prepared questions for the involved developers with the AI Office. The release says recommendations would be presented at a special meeting, but does not identify the incidents, publish the questions or recommendations, or report regulatory follow-through. This is the Commission’s account of planned advisory work, not independent incident verification or a new binding rule. — FCMO-CA575C0CC53D

Anthropic revises its Usage Policy with explicit rules for deceptive campaigns and high-risk physical actions — importance 5/10 · Anthropic’s updated Usage Policy, marked effective November 12, 2026, adds explicit requirements for users connecting its models to hardware capable of high-risk physical actions: a qualified person must be able to observe and stop equipment, which must enter or hold a safe state if the person intervenes or service connectivity is lost. The revision also has a separate prohibition on deceptive campaigns and artificial activity, including fake personas, concealed sponsorship and networks of ostensibly independent sites. Comparison with Anthropic’s archived September 15, 2025 policy confirms the physical-action controls are new to this document. This is a provider usage policy, not a law; enforcement and resulting safety outcomes are unverified. — FCMO-E77F93F0C039

UK ICO reports developer privacy commitments and opens an agentic-AI evidence call — importance 5/10 · On 8 October 2026, the UK Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) said ten major foundation-model developers operating in the country had made or committed to changes on transparency, people’s data rights and safeguards. Its linked supervision report gives named examples: it says Anthropic and OpenAI updated legitimate-interest assessments, Meta supplied additional evidence including memorisation-testing results, and Apple and DeepSeek have some commitments still to complete. The ICO also opened a six-week call for evidence on agentic-AI data-protection risks, closing 20 November, and said enquiries into OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and the UK AI Security Institute over earlier testing and deployment remain ongoing. The regulator’s report is not an independent audit, and neither the commitments nor enquiries establish reduced risk or violations. — FCMO-697CC69F3A11

NIST finalizes signed-token protections that explicitly cover AI agents and workloads — importance 4/10 · NIST IR 8587, finalized September 15, 2026 with CISA participation, provides implementation recommendations for signed identity tokens and assertions. Section 1.1.1 says organizations should apply the guidance when AI agents use signed tokens to access systems, data, tools, or APIs. Section 5.3.1.6 says workload identities must use tightly scoped, short-lived tokens issued through approved enterprise identity platforms, and should use sender-constrained mechanisms when feasible. The report says it is not a comprehensive guide to AI-agent access risks and that further guidance is being developed. — FCMO-2B53E683F72E

items: ANVIL separates LLM formulation from deterministic optimization-code compilation — importance 4/10 · The authors introduce ANVIL, which uses an LLM once to formulate an LP/MILP in LaTeX and then compiles that representation through a typed, deterministic pipeline into PuLP code. On 354 easy and hard NLP4LP benchmark problems, the paper reports deterministic compilation for 329 (92.9%) with no model-code fallback; among 320 problems with numeric references, 299 matched (93.4%). These are author-reported results from one arXiv preprint, not an independent reproduction. — FCMO-1BE32AB7A431
